title: OCP Summit 2026: Powering AI with Open Innovations in Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across Networks
abstract: At the 2026 Open Compute Project Global Summit, Meta is sharing the next generation of open networking infrastructure, including: Our first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack), and 102.4T switch platform (IceCube). Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), a multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network MetaRoCE, our open-source AI transport protocol. Launching the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) initiative within OCP. We’re inviting engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in meeting the challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI infrastructure. At Meta, we believe that open networking is critical for building high-performance, scalable, and sustainable infrastructure, and we’ve acted on that conviction since co-founding the Open Compute Project (OCP) in 2011. Throughout the ongoing AI revolution, Meta has pushed the boundaries of what’s possible in data center networking and shared our advances with the industry. At OCP 2025, we introduced our latest AI scale-out fabrics and drove the creation of the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) initiative. This year at OCP 2026, we’re sharing the networking innovations that directly support our latest AI workloads such as Meta’s Muse Wonder and Muse Spark models, and Muse, our personal AI agent built for everyone . Here’s some of what’s new: The 102.4T scale-out switch : Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack) and 102.4T switch blades (IceCube), designed to support high power density, deliver higher thermal efficiency, and enable gigawatt-scale AI clusters. The scale-out Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF) : Meta’s multiplane fabric, enabling larger, highly efficient GPU clusters with lower latency — with learnings shared with our cloud partners. Scale-across for multi-site clusters : Meta’s petabit-scale backend aggregation (BAG) super-spine and how large-scale training jobs deal with failures at this scale — with an overview of how we’ve built SRv6 regional backbones using FBOSS and SAI to handle even longer distances Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking: Meta’s MTIA 300 system uses Tahan, an Ethernet-based 51.2T scale-up switch, delivering 6.4 Tbps per accelerator — with a preview of next-gen 72-accelerator-per-rack design on 102.4T silicon and moving toward an ESUN-based implementation with future chips. Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) : a new OCP initiative, co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba, that standardizes the switch platform layer — with specification v1.0 now submitted to OCP. MetaRoCE : Meta’s RDMA transport protocol for AI networks — now with open-source implementations. The 102.4T Generation: Liquid-Cooled Networking at AI Scale As AI clusters grow to gigawatt scale, network switches must deliver dramatically more bandwidth while fitting within increasingly dense power and cooling envelopes. Our answer is the IcePack rack, Meta’s first-generation liquid-cooled network rack. IcePack is based on OCP’s ORV3-HPRv1 rack standard . IceCube switch blades — 102.4-Tbps fabric switches that deliver 128×800G non-blocking switching capacity — sit inside each rack. IceCube comes in two variants , one built on Broadcom’s Tomahawk6C switch ASIC and one on NVIDIA Spectrum-6 Switch ASIC. Both run Meta’s open-source FBOSS network operating system that leverages OCP SAI (Switch Abstraction Interface). This new generation represents a 2x bandwidth increase over our 51.2T platforms while achieving the thermal density required for next-generation AI data centers. title: Shipping Media Over QUIC at Meta Scale for Instagram Live Ingest
abstract: Meta has begun deploying Media over QUIC (MoQ), an emerging open protocol for real-time video streaming at scale. MoQ will help simplify our protocol stack for live streaming video and enhance overall user experience for live video. We’re sharing how we shipped MoQ on Instagram Live ingest, and what the future looks like from here. This work was also presented at DEMOQED 2026 . Instagram Live now uses the open standard transport protocol Media over QUIC (MoQ) for live video ingest on iOS and Android. As a transport designed for both ingest and playback, MoQ gives us the foundation to build toward an architecture that is lower-latency, more resilient on unreliable networks, and more responsive for creators and viewers. It also gives teams across Meta a common foundation for bringing those improvements to future live and interactive experiences without rebuilding them on separate protocol stacks. MoQ: A Media Protocol for Every Moment in Time The internet has accumulated a rich set of media protocols, each shaped by the problem in front of it. RTMP for ingestion. HLS and DASH for playback. WebRTC for real-time calls. RUSH for the cases that did not fit neatly into any of those. Each was a strong answer for its moment, and together they’ve carried the industry a long way. At Meta, someone who starts a live stream and then makes a voice call on the same app touches three different protocol stacks, each with its own serving infrastructure, monitoring, and operational expertise. That separation made sense when these experiences were distinct. But as live video, real-time AI, and generative AI creation tools increasingly share the same product surface, the lines between these use cases are starting to blur. A common protocol across ingest, delivery, and playback can reduce the number of custom transports and operating models that engineering teams need to maintain and improve over time. How MoQ Works MoQ is an emerging IETF standard that enables low-latency, scalable media delivery (live streaming, real-time communication) over the QUIC transport layer. It’s being developed collaboratively at the IETF, with active participation from Meta, Google, Akamai, Cisco, Cloudflare, and academia. For nearly a decade, Meta’s live streaming video has run on Reliable Ultra-low-latency Streaming over HTTP (RUSH), an in-house QUIC-based protocol built to move past RTMP. RUSH proved that QUIC could carry live media at scale and was a predecessor to MoQ. The lessons learned from running RUSH in production are part of what shaped our bet on MoQ. The core abstraction in MoQ is a Track , an addressable stream of media objects that publishers push and subscribers receive through a network of relays. Relays cache and forward objects without parsing the media payload – they only need to understand the MoQ framing and delivery metadata. A few properties matter for using MoQ as a single transport across the full latency spectrum: Built on QUIC: QUIC lets independent streams make progress without TCP-style cross-stream head-of-line blocking. It also supports faster connection setup and connection migration. Meta’s earlier QUIC rollout achieved lower request errors, tail latency, and video stalls than HTTP/2. MoQ applies the same transport foundation to live and real-time media. MoQ would also automatically benefit from any feature added to QUIC (e.g., FEC). Native Fan-out and caching: MoQ relays are built-in caching and request/stream coalescing endpoints, so media streams scale through CDN relays out of the box. Request coalescing, caching, and fan-out are not new (live streaming already does them), but MoQ makes them part of the protocol design rather than a bolt-on, and it is designed to scale via relays more efficiently than traditional HTTP streaming. title: Turning Opportunistic AI Inference Capacity Into Better Ads Recommendations
abstract: At Meta, we’ve built a system that enhances ads recommendations by leveraging idle inference capacity in our fleet. Two elasticity levers in the system allow ads recommendation work to expand across opportunistic capacity, without compromising baseline performance. This post describes how we designed and now operate the system at Meta’s scale and how it drives significant advertiser value and capacity efficiency. Inference fleets face a capacity paradox: They can be globally constrained while meaningful pockets of capacity remain locally idle. At Meta, we built a system that aggregates these pockets into a shared opportunistic capacity pool and turns them into better ads recommendations. By putting otherwise idle capacity to work, the system helps people see more relevant ads and improves advertiser outcomes without requiring additional capacity orders. Using this opportunistic capacity safely is difficult. It’s distributed across team-owned capacity allocations, regions, and accelerator types, and may be reclaimed with little notice. The ads inference system must therefore adapt workload as capacity supply changes without overloading the dedicated capacity that serves baseline workload. We address this challenge with two complementary elasticity levers. Rank More Ads (RMA) adjusts the number of candidates evaluated by the ranking stages. Serve Better Models (SBM) adjusts the share of requests routed to a more powerful model. Physical and logical isolation protects the capacity reserved for baseline serving. Separate feedback loops control RMA candidate volume and SBM model coverage, while value-aware load shedding at both servers and clients allows the system to degrade gracefully when capacity is suddenly reclaimed. Together, these mechanisms allow optional work to expand and contract with opportunistic capacity while protecting latency and reliability. The Inference Capacity Paradox: Globally Constrained, but Locally Idle Inference fleets must maintain enough capacity to meet demand under strict latency and reliability targets. However, demand and capacity rarely align perfectly across time, regions, resource combinations, and accelerator types. Capacity can therefore remain idle in parts of a fleet even when the fleet is constrained overall. Common causes include: Peak-provisioning and demand-variation mismatch: Inference fleets must be provisioned for peak demand, while traffic varies by time of day and season. Capacity needed during peak periods can therefore remain temporarily idle when demand is lower. Model-development and capacity-delivery timing mismatch: Inference capacity arrives on supply-chain timelines, whereas models are developed and launched on separate schedules. This creates a gap between when capacity becomes available and when models are ready to consume it. Regional resource-ratio mismatch: Inference workloads require accelerators as well as supporting resources such as CPUs. When these resources are not available in the required proportions, one resource can remain idle while another limits serving capacity. Accelerator-type mismatch: Inference fleets can span multiple accelerator vendors, generations, and architectures. Workloads are not always portable across these accelerator types, which can strand capacity on hardware that cannot immediately serve the available demand. These mismatches create an industry-wide inference capacity paradox: A fleet can be globally constrained while meaningful pockets of capacity remain locally idle. At Meta’s scale, these temporary pockets can collectively represent substantial capacity and create better ads recommendations when used safely. From Fragmented Reservations to a Shared Opportunistic Capacity Pool Across a heterogeneous fleet at Meta’s scale, instantaneous idle inference capacity is inevitable — even with proactive planning designed to minimize structural mismatches. title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
abstract: At a glance StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration. StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. Figure 1: AI tutors need feedback from students to improve. Student simulators can approximate part of that feedback during research-stage training and evaluation. They provide an early-stage research signal, not a replacement for testing with real learners. Measuring what a student simulator needs to do A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable. Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question. title: Can we change an AI model’s architecture without retraining it from scratch?
abstract: AI agents are rapidly scaling: longer sessions, deeper reasoning chains, more autonomy. But the Transformer architecture underneath them still pays a memory tax that grows with the number of tokens it processes. As agents become more capable, that cost scales with them. Now, there’s a proliferation of hybrid architectures that use some combination of methods to achieve a better balance of memory, speed, and quality. Those methods include sparse attention, which selects a subset of past tokens to consider when selecting the next token; sliding-window attention, which preserves only the most recent tokens; and state space models, which compress information from the full history into a fixed-size state. These hybrid architectures can be understood as points in a sequence-model design space: to differing degrees, they mix information while traversing a sequence and passing through different states. What distinguishes them from each other is how they retain and use the past. Until now, exploring this design space has required training every new architecture from scratch, using trillions of tokens and hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours. This has made controlled comparisons of hybrid architectures extremely expensive. In a new paper, “Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers,” our team at Amazon Web Services addresses this problem. We introduce priming, a method that leverages pretrained Transformer weights as a starting point to reduce the pretraining cost of hybrid architectures by more than 99%. With priming, model developers can ask questions that were previously too expensive to answer at scale: Which attention layers can be replaced by more-efficient layers? How many attention layers can be replaced without sacrificing quality? Which state space layer works best? And what does the trade-off between speed and accuracy look like? In our paper, we compare hybrid models that use three different types of state space models (Gated KalmaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba-2). Some of our findings: Not all state space models are equal. Under controlled conditions, Gated KalmaNet (GKA) performs best, followed by Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and then Mamba-2. GKA uniquely offers variable-length inference computation without retraining and gives the user direct control over its position on the speed-accuracy frontier. A good lossy summary of everything beats a perfect recording of the most recent past. State space models consistently outperform sliding-window attention (SWA), even when SWA gets twice the memory budget. Same quality, twice the throughput. A 32-billion-parameter GKA-based hybrid model matches its source Transformer on reasoning benchmarks while decoding up to twice as quickly with 128,000 tokens of context and reaching correct answers in as little as two-thirds of the wall-clock time. To foster further research on hybrid architectures, we have released a zoo of primed hybrid models at the eight-billion-parameter and 32-billion-parameter scales for long-context reasoning and instruction following, together with training code, optimized kernels, and a vLLM-serving plugin under the Apache 2.0 License. The attention mechanism A Transformer’s attention mechanism — which determines how relevant previously seen tokens are to the token currently being processed — relies on three different vectors, which take their names from database design: the query, the key, and the value. For each token, the query captures what that token is “looking for,” the key captures what it “offers,” and the value carries the actual information it will pass along. Relevance is computed by comparing the current token’s query against every other token’s key; the closer the match, the more that token’s value contributes to the output of attention. Each of these vectors is produced by multiplying the token by a learned weight projection matrix. title: Accessing OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock with global cross-Region inference in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan
abstract: Single-Region inference can throttle when demand exceeds local capacity. Teams in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan need access to the newest OpenAI models beyond that capacity. Amazon Bedrock offers OpenAI GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna through global cross-Region inference from all five AWS Regions, and GPT-6 Astra from Asia Pacific (Singapore). This post shows you how to configure the call, set permissions, and monitor inference from your source Region. GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6 Astra are all available through global cross-Region inference from the preceding Regions, on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. See Cross-Region inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. For the full list of source and destination Regions in each profile, see Supported Regions and models for inference profiles . In this post, we introduce the global cross-Region inference profiles and invoke them from Asia Pacific (Singapore) using the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, and coding clients. We then cover the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and service control policy (SCP) configuration, quota management, and monitoring. Global cross-Region inference profiles for OpenAI GPT-6 The GPT-6 family offers three models, each available through global cross-Region inference. GPT-6 Sol brings strong reasoning and coding capabilities to complex tasks performed throughout the week. GPT-6 Luna makes focused, repeatable tasks practical at high volume. GPT-6 Astra handles complex reasoning, coding, and long-document work. All three accept text and image input, client-side tool use, and prompt caching. They differ on reasoning effort. GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna accept none, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. GPT-6 Astra accepts the same levels except none. For GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, see Bring more intelligence to everyday work with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on Amazon Bedrock . For GPT-6 Astra, see Take on your most ambitious work with GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock . Global cross-Region inference routes requests across supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed, giving you broad access to Amazon Bedrock capacity. You invoke it by passing a global cross-Region inference profile ID in place of a model ID. Your source Region is where you make the API call. Amazon Bedrock selects the destination Region for processing. Billing, quota tracking, AWS CloudTrail, and Amazon CloudWatch all stay in your source Region. title: Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: Applications that route requests, select agent actions, or assign policy outcomes often need scores over a fixed set of choices instead of free-form text. Deploying these decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI gives you a managed path for serving quantized models on CPU or GPU infrastructure. This post continues a series on specialized AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) for generative AI inference. Previous posts cover WhisperX , vLLM-Omni – Part 1 , and vLLM-Omni – Part 2 . In this post, you first use the AWS DLC for llama.cpp to serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through SageMaker AI InvokeEndpoint . You then extend the same runtime with SemIf , formerly OpenJev, which returns probabilities over declared options without decoding an answer token. The accompanying code sample includes CPU and GPU deployment options. Solution overview Figure 1 shows two deployment paths from the same packaged model. The text-generation path uses the AWS DLC for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI-compatible API. The structured-decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options. Figure 1: Run the AWS DLC for llama.cpp or the SemIf child image on CPU or GPU, depending on the API and latency requirements of your workload For the standard path, package the model as model.tar.gz in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference the published DLC image directly. The container finds the first .gguf file under /opt/ml/model , maps POST /invocations to llama-server at /v1/chat/completions , and passes SM_LLAMA_CPP_* environment variables to llama.cpp arguments. The llama-server HTTP API doesn’t expose the final-position logits and state operations that SemIf uses. The structured-decision path therefore uses AWS CodeBuild to build a child image and store it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . The child image keeps the DLC’s compiled CPU or CUDA libraries while replacing its entry point with a SageMaker-compatible adapter. Understand the input and output schemas The AWS DLC for llama.cpp accepts the OpenAI Chat Completions schema. Send a messages array with role and content , plus generation controls such as max_tokens and stream : { "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "A customer cannot receive a password reset email. Reply with the best support queue." } ], "max_tokens": 64, "stream": false } The response uses the OpenAI-compatible choices array. Read generated text from choices[0].message.content . SemIf uses a constrained decision schema instead of chat messages. The request contains a caller-defined ID, unstructured state, a question, and an ordered list of allowed options: { "decision": { "id": "support-route", "state": "The customer cannot receive a password reset email.", "question": "Which queue should handle this request?", "options": [ {"id": "account_access", "description": "Account access support."}, {"id": "billing", "description": "Billing support."} ] } } The response returns option_ids , probabilities , and raw option_logits in the same order, along with prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata. With stable option IDs, your application can apply thresholds, fallbacks, and policy checks without parsing generated prose. SemIf belongs to a broader class of decision models that score application-defined outcomes from unstructured state. title: Run multi-node inference workloads using Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers
abstract: This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with the multi-node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers . It uses separate prefill and decode nodes behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. This kind of multi-node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads. In a previous post , we introduced the Ray Serve DLC and used it to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node. You had a working inference endpoint, and the container keeps the GPU stack compatible, including CUDA libraries, so you did not need to write boilerplate code. Ray is a distributed compute framework, so Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes. Customers use multi-node Ray Serve for several reasons. Some want to run foundation or open-weight models that are too large for a single GPU. Others need more throughput than one replica can deliver. Still others want to separate the two phases of inference to improve performance. In each case, customers must build the dependency chain themselves: choosing compatible libraries for the GPU stack and debugging issues when a component drifts out of alignment. This is undifferentiated work that takes time and effort away from delivering models. AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) have long solved this kind of problem for training and inferencing workloads. DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. With the launch of the Ray LLM DLC for multi-node deployments, that same approach now extends to multi-node inference. You get a container purpose-built for serving models behind an HTTP endpoint, maintained and tested by AWS, with the full inference stack already assembled. This post walks through implementing multi-node disaggregated inference using multi-node Ray LLM DLC: deploying a single large language model across two GPU-powered nodes on Amazon EKS cooperating behind a single endpoint. While one of the GPU nodes handles the prefill phase, the other GPU node handles the decode phase. Separating the phases prevents compute-heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress. This approach is well suited for workloads such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), document summarization, and agentic applications. We use the multi-node Ray LLM DLC, which ships Ray Serve LLM , NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL) , and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with no application code. The complete code is available in the accompanying repository . Why prefill/decode (PD) disaggregation LLM inference has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input prompt in parallel and builds the key-value (KV) cache. Decode then generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending that cache. Prefill is compute bound, and Decode is bound by memory bandwidth. When both phases share one GPU, they contend for the same resources, and the bursty, compute-heavy prefill work interferes with the steady, latency-sensitive decode work. Separating the prefill phase from the decode phase means you can select the hardware and serving properties for each phase, improving overall performance at scale. PD disaggregation places the two phases on separate nodes, so each phase runs without interfering with the other and can be scaled independently. The trade-off is that the KV cache built during prefill must be handed to the decode node, and that transfer should be fast enough not to erase the benefit. That is exactly why the interconnect between the nodes matters. abstract: Long agent traces composed of chains of thought and tool calls accumulate stale content that anchor subsequent generations, and eventually outgrow the context window. Zero to Agent in 30 Minutes: Build a Personal Assistant on OpenClaw
abstract: In the final episode of Zero to Agent in 30 Minutes , AI engineer Sajal Sharma showed how to build a personal assistant on OpenClaw that tracks your tasks and notes and handles scheduled work on its own. A useful personal assistant has to be reachable when you’re away from your computer and keep running when it has scheduled work to do. OpenClaw supports both, and you decide where the agent runs, which models it uses, and how it accesses your data. How to go from a fresh install to scheduled automations, step-by-step Install your OpenClaw instance. Sajal recommends starting locally while you learn how it works, then moving to an always-on machine or hosted environment if you need continuous availability. Connect the channels you use. Add a messaging channel such as Telegram, WhatsApp, or Slack so you can reach the assistant away from your desk. Sajal used Telegram in his demo to send requests and receive notifications from the same assistant. Set up the assistant’s workspace. Give the agent a place to keep tasks, notes, skills, and memory, along with guidance files that define how it behaves and how it should work with the files in that workspace. Use it in your daily workflows. Sajal asked the assistant for an overview of current projects and checked progress toward a reading goal. He also had it search the web for a book series and add the books it found to his reading list. Add proactive automations. Schedule work the assistant should handle on its own. Sajal added a Telegram reminder and a morning briefing designed to pull from tasks, a calendar, and recent email. title: Designing Websites for People and AI Agents with WebMCP
abstract: The following article originally appeared on the Agentic AI Foundation blog and is being reposted here with the author’s permission. Websites are designed for people. We can look at a page and quickly understand where to enter information or which control will complete an action. AI agents don’t see or use the web the same way we do. An agent may have to process a screenshot or inspect the page’s underlying structure, then reason about which control matches the request. The additional context increases token use, and each interpretation step creates another chance for error. WebMCP (not to be confused with MCP) gives web developers a standard way to publish structured tools to access the capabilities of their website enabling agents to call those functions with structured inputs. A developer can register a tool through document.modelContext and give it a name and description. The tool also defines an input schema and the function that runs when an agent calls it. For example, an article site could publish a search tool that calls the same application code as its visible search form. const searchToolController = new AbortController(); await document.modelContext.registerTool( { name: "search-articles", title: "Search articles", description: "Search published articles by topic.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { query: { type: "string", description: "The topic or phrase to search for." } }, required: ["query"], additionalProperties: false }, async execute({ query }) { const articles = await searchArticles(query); renderSearchResults(articles); return { articles }; } }, { signal: searchToolController.signal } ); // Call this when the search tool should no longer be available. // searchToolController.abort(); The name and description tell the agent when to use the tool. The input schema defines the arguments it can send. The execute function calls the site’s existing search logic and updates the page with the results. The browser makes the registered tool available to a supported agent while the page is active. When the agent calls it, the browser passes the structured arguments to execute and returns the result. When the search tool should no longer be available, the page can unregister it by calling searchToolController.abort() . A page registers tools that match its current state. A content view may provide a search tool, while an editor can provide tools for changing the selected content. The agent then discovers the tools available for the page’s current state. WebMCP also proposes a declarative path for existing HTML forms. The article search could be exposed through attributes on the form itself. <form action="/articles" method="get" toolname="search-articles" tooldescription="Search published articles by topic." > <label for="article-query">Topic</label> <input id="article-query" name="query" type="search" toolparamdescription="The topic or phrase to search for." required > <button type="submit">Search</button> </form> The browser uses the form attributes and controls to create the tool definition. Because the form omits toolautosubmit , the browser populates the field but leaves the final click to the person. The person can review the search query and click the Search button. Keep the person and agent in the same interface A WebMCP tool uses the state already visible in the application and the person’s active session. The shared page gives the person a place to review the agent’s work. When the agent completes an action, the person can see the updated state and make changes through the normal interface. Web developers can also reuse application logic that already handles the visible interface. OpenAI’s Runme example is a browser application that registers tools for reading instructions and updating notebook content. title: Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
abstract: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars. The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements . If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones , robotic landers, communication satellites , and a nuclear power plant ; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water. Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.” The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved? But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher. SELMAN DESIGN But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales. Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán. title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
abstract: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth. Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land . As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records. That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba , hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest. The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife. Filling in the gaps Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees , after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way? While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs , Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. title: Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy
abstract: If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone. Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs. Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San Francisco Title Member of technical staff Member grade IEEE senior member Alma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India “My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications. Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement , the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models , Saran says. “We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.” Solving data quality problems at Yahoo, Intuit, and Meta Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab. “I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity. “That felt magical to me.” After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani . In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani. While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions. “We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.” The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more. With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic. From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits , an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products. Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. title: Long-lost horror gaming cult classic P.T. gets a much-needed PC port
abstract: For over a decade now, the only "official" way to play Hideo Kojima's cult classic, P.T. —the long-discontinued "playable trailer" for Kojima's canceled "Silent Hills" project —has been via one of the increasingly rare PlayStation 4s that previously downloaded a copy during its monthslong availability window. Now, though, one coder is helping to preserve the game with a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable from the original PS4 files. Coder Lorean Xavier said he was inspired to work on the "P.T. for PC" project "because P.T. deserved to keep existing somewhere other than on consoles that still have it installed." The open source porting effort rebuilds the P.T. engine in C++ and Vulkan, using the original files from the PS4 game to re-create "every level, model, texture, sound, script and cutscene," according to its GitHub listing. That means players without their own legitimate decrypted copy of the original P.T. will have to track one down in order to generate a playable PC version. The reliance on real P.T. files makes this port more authentic than previous hobbyist efforts to re-create the look and feel of P.T. for a PC audience. And while PS4 emulators recently reached a point where they could run P.T. completely , this native port also sports extra features, like upscaling and frame-generation, a camera mode, experimental third-person and VR support, and a "museum" section where you can look at and listen to in-game assets (including "unused content"). title: F1 in Singapore: There's a new fastest car now
abstract: Formula 1’s lengthy 2026 season is entering its final stretch. The sport took to the floodlit streets of Singapore on Sunday night, but Saturday saw action, too; this Grand Prix weekend was also the final of six sprints this year. The night race might be one of modern F1’s greatest spectacles. From overhead shots, the track becomes a bright, illuminated ribbon among the looming darkness of the city-state’s overpasses and skyscrapers. At ground level, the cars shower glittering sparks from their titanium skid blocks as the drivers flirt with how close they can get to the walls. As tracks go, the 90-degree turns and concrete barrier-lined streets were a world away from the abrasive tarmac and ample runoff of Malaysia last time out . But the tropical heat and humidity were a constant given both locations’ proximity to the equator. Showers for the sprint In Malaysia (which was still technically the Bahrain GP), a pre-race downpour disrupted things mightily. On Saturday morning in Singapore, shortly before the start of the sprint, it seemed history was about to rhyme when the skies opened. With standing water in places on the track, the sprint was delayed by 30 minutes. The sprint format, where a short extra race replaces a practice session a day before the main event, is unloved by the drivers and teams. For one thing, there’s little prestige in winning Saturday’s sprint. And with qualifying just a few hours later, risk-taking is discouraged lest one wreck the car and ruin Sunday’s race a day early. Oh no, not again! Credit: Mark Thompson/Getty Images And in Singapore, like most street circuits, the proximity of the unyielding barriers that line the track means there are real, punishing consequences for getting it even a little wrong. abstract: Google is releasing its second Fitbit tracker of 2026, offering fans of the aging Charge 6 a more refined option. The new Fitbit Edge slots right in between the Pixel Watch 5 and the Fitbit Air , featuring a compact screen and more health sensors than the Air. You won't get all the apps and features of the Pixel Watch 5, but the Edge is only about half as expensive. The Fitbit Edge is essentially a new Charge 6, but it has more of a Pixel Watch aesthetic. Squish Google's smartwatch from the sides, and you've got the Edge. It has a pill-shaped 1.34-inch OLED touch display inside a slender aluminum frame that is rated IP68 (5 ATM) for water and dust protection. Google says the screen has 46 percent more viewable area compared to the Charge 6. It's very close in overall size to the Fitbit Air and uses the same magnetic charging puck. Left to right: Fitbit Air (with new metal mesh band), Fitbit Edge, and Pixel Watch 5. Credit: Google The Edge works with Android or iPhones via the Google Health app, and it can run for about seven days on a charge. If the tracker is away from your phone, it can still follow your activity all week with support for seven days of full health data storage (or 30 days of basic data). However, the generous weeklong battery life does not include always-on display mode. If you turn it on, battery life drops to about two days, barely longer than the Pixel Watch 5. title: Amazon has over 1 million robot workers. What’s next for human employees?
abstract: No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers. Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report . Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots. “For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we've seen usually happens away from workers—you're taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you're doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood , professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.” Read full article Comments

title: 서비스 개발에 집중할 수 있는 AI 플랫폼 만들기
abstract: 생성형 AI로 기능을 만들기 위해 모델을 호출하는 것은 어렵지 않습니다. 하지만 실제 서비스에 적용하려면 사용할 모델과 데이터의 처리 범위를 정하고, 예상 비용과 필요한 처리 용량도 검토해야 합니다. 서비스 팀마다 이 과정을 따로 준비하면 비슷한 작업을 반복하게 됩니다. 모델 공급자별 연동 코드를 작성하고, 권한을 확인하고, 사용량을 집계해야 하죠. 운영을 시작한 뒤에는 호출이 왜 실패했는지, 요청이 몰릴 때 어떻게 처리할지도 고민해야 합니다. 토스 AI Platform 팀은 이 중 여러 서비스에 공통으로 필요한 일을 플랫폼이 맡도록 했습니다. 서비스 팀이 사용 목적과 필요한 모델을 정하면, 검토한 조건을 실제 호출에 적용하고 그 결과를 운영 중에도 확인할 수 있게 만드는 데 초점을 맞췄습니다. GenAI Portal은 모델 사용 신청과 설정을 관리하는 웹 서비스입니다. 실제 호출은 서비스와 모델 사이에서 요청을 처리하는 LLM Gateway 서버인 GenAI Gateway가 맡습니다. Portal에서 정한 사용 조건을 Gateway가 실제 요청에 적용하도록 연결했습니다. 사내 도구를 호출할 때는 MCP Gateway가 실행 권한을 확인합니다. 검토한 사용 조건을 실제 호출까지 연결하기 서비스에 맞는 모델을 찾았더라도 바로 사용할 수 있는 것은 아닙니다. 성능이 충분하더라도 처리할 데이터와 실행 환경에 맞는지 확인해야 하고, 예상 요청량을 감당할 용량도 필요합니다. Portal에서는 위 화면처럼 필요한 비교 항목을 골라 모델별 가격과 사양을 살펴볼 수 있습니다. 가격과 성능을 함께 비교할 때는 리더보드를 사용합니다. 가로축과 세로축에 비교할 지표를 선택해 모델별 차이를 볼 수 있습니다. 공개 벤치마크 점수와 사내 서빙 환경에서 측정한 응답 지연 시간은 구분해 제공합니다. 사용할 모델을 정하면 프로젝트에서 사용을 신청합니다. 권한과 비용을 관리하는 단위도 바로 이 프로젝트입니다. 위 화면처럼 처리할 데이터의 등급과 서비스 중단 시 영향을 입력하도록 안내합니다. 담당자와 실행 환경, 사용할 모델, 예산과 사용량 제한을 프로젝트에 등록한 뒤 API 키를 발급받습니다. 키가 여러 개여도 같은 프로젝트라면 모델 권한과 예산을 함께 관리하고 사용량도 합쳐서 볼 수 있습니다. 서비스의 운영 조건이 개별 키마다 흩어지지 않도록 통일하고 있습니다. 금융 서비스에 필요한 검토도 이 프로젝트를 기준으로 진행합니다. 담당자가 사용 목적과 데이터 처리 범위를 정하면 담당 조직이 검토하고, 혁신금융서비스의 허용 범위에 맞는지 확인합니다. 모델을 추가하거나 사용량 한도를 바꿀 때도 변경 내용을 신청하고 필요한 승인을 받습니다. 위 화면처럼 추가할 모델과 변경 전후의 사용량 한도, 예산을 보여주고 신청 사유와 함께 검토할 수 있도록 했습니다. 승인 결과는 프로젝트 설정에 반영하고, 모델과 공급자 정보, 변경 이력도 Portal에서 확인할 수 있습니다. 신청자가 가이드를 미리 읽지 않아도 필요한 내용을 알 수 있도록, 각 단계의 안내도 실제 사용 과정에서 겪는 불편을 바탕으로 다듬고 있습니다. 데이터 등급은 실제로 다루는 정보 중 가장 민감한 항목을 기준으로 정합니다. 토스 내부 기준에서는 다음과 같이 구분합니다. L1: 주민등록번호와 계좌번호 등 최고 민감 정보 L2: 일반 개인정보와 개인신용정보, 행태로그 L3: 영업비밀과 가명화한 개인정보 L4: 익명화 정보와 집계정보 등급이 같더라도 데이터를 쓰는 목적과 환경은 다를 수 있습니다. 그래서 등급만으로 사용을 허가하지 않고, 사용할 모델과 실행 환경을 함께 검토합니다. 서비스는 모델을 지정하고, Gateway는 호출을 처리합니다 검토한 조건은 요청을 받을 때도 확인해야 합니다. GenAI Gateway는 API 키로 요청 프로젝트임을 인증하고, 활성 상태와 모델 사용 권한을 확인합니다. 사용량 한도와 입력 가드레일을 통과한 요청만 모델로 전달합니다. 여기서 서비스가 지정하는 모델과 실제 요청을 처리하는 배포를 구분했습니다. 같은 모델이라도 공급자와 배포 환경에 따라 호출 조건이 다르기 때문입니다. Gateway는 해당 혁신금융서비스 정책에 따른 공급자 설정과 배포 상태를 반영해 호출할 곳을 선택합니다. 공급자별 인증과 요청 형식 변환은 어댑터가 맡고, 권한 확인과 사용량 제한은 공통 로직으로 분리했습니다. 공급자가 늘어날 때마다 서비스에서 이런 제어를 다시 구현하지 않아도 되도록 만든 것입니다. 사내 GPU에서 운영하는 모델도 같은 Gateway를 통해 호출합니다. 이 경우 모델 서빙은 자체 플랫폼인 Toss Dynamo가 담당합니다. 다만 호출 형식을 맞춰도 모델의 기능까지 같아지지는 않습니다. 도구 호출이나 구조화된 출력 지원 여부는 서비스에서 모델을 선택할 때 따로 살펴봐야 합니다. 모델을 호출할 권한과 사내 도구를 실행할 권한은 별개입니다. 그림처럼 모델 호출은 GenAI Gateway를, 도구 호출은 MCP Gateway를 거치도록 나눴습니다. 하나의 MCP(Model Context Protocol) 서버에는 여러 도구를 등록할 수 있습니다. 등록할 때는 기술적 보안 요건과 개인정보 처리 등급, 데이터 처리 방식을 검토합니다. 등록을 마친 도구도 프로젝트에서 사용을 신청해야 목적에 맞는 권한을 부여받을 수 있습니다. MCP Gateway는 호출마다 프로젝트와 서버, RPC 메서드, 도구 이름을 확인해 실행을 허용할지 판단합니다. 도구 실행 권한과 데이터 접근 권한은 여기서도 구분해야 합니다. 검색 도구를 실행할 수 있다고 해서 모든 문서를 읽을 수 있는 것은 아니니까요. 도구 실행 여부는 MCP Gateway가 판단하지만, 데이터 접근 권한은 연결된 서비스에서 별도로 확인해야 합니다. 터미널이나 코딩 에이전트에서 개발할 때는 GenAI CLI로 모델 목록과 등록된 MCP 도구를 조회할 수 있습니다. 웹 화면을 열지 않고도 개발 중에 필요한 정보를 찾아볼 수 있도록 했습니다. 본문을 보호하면서도 문제를 추적할 수 있어야 합니다 사용 범위를 검토해 두어도 실제 요청에는 예상하지 못한 정보가 섞일 수 있습니다. 사용자가 자유롭게 입력한 글이나 외부 문서를 다룬다면 특히 그렇습니다. 이때 승인된 처리 범위를 지키기 위해 외부 모델 호출 전에 가드레일로 입력을 검사합니다. 하지만 요청을 차단해도 본문이 일반 로그에 그대로 남으면 보호할 정보가 다른 경로로 노출될 수 있습니다. 반대로 기록을 모두 없애면 운영 중 문제가 생겼을 때 원인을 찾기 어렵습니다. 그림에서 모델로 전달하는 경로와 로그를 남기는 경로를 나눈 이유입니다. 모델 호출 전에는 프롬프트 공격과 개인정보를 검사합니다. 개인정보는 규칙과 문맥을 판단하는 모델로 찾고, 탐지 결과가 프로젝트의 차단 조건에 해당하면 호출을 중단합니다. 응답 검사를 지원하는 API에서는 차단 대상인 응답도 반환하지 않습니다. 로그를 남길 때는 본문과 운영 정보를 구분합니다. 일반 운영 로그를 전송하기 전에 규칙이나 모델이 탐지한 개인정보 영역을 마스킹합니다. 프로젝트 설정에 따라 본문을 기록하지 않을 수도 있습니다. 본문을 가리더라도 호출 상태와 지연 시간, 사용량, 실패한 단계는 따로 확인할 수 있게 했습니다. 무엇을 탐지했는지와 실제로 차단했는지도 구분해 남깁니다. 같은 유형을 탐지해도 프로젝트 설정에 따라 처리 결과가 달라질 수 있기 때문입니다. 보안 검토용 기록은 일반 운영 로그와 목적과 처리 경로를 구분해 관리합니다. 여기까지는 개별 모델 호출의 기록입니다. 문서를 검색한 뒤 모델을 여러 번 호출하는 서비스라면, 어느 단계에서 시간이 오래 걸렸는지 파악하려면 서비스 전체 흐름이 필요합니다. 서비스 전체 흐름은 Langfuse 트레이스로 확인하고, Gateway 로그에도 서비스가 전달한 같은 추적 식별자를 남깁니다. 전체 처리 과정을 보다가 특정 모델 호출이 궁금하면 같은 식별자로 상세 기록을 찾을 수 있습니다. 연동을 시작하는 과정도 사내 배포 환경에 맞췄습니다. title: CPU 뼛속까지 써먹고, Milvus 사이징 기준을 만들기까지
abstract: 안녕하세요. 토스증권 Data Infra 팀 장재영입니다. 토스증권에서는 벡터 검색 워크로드를 지원하기 위해 Milvus 기반의 검색 환경을 구성했는데요. 실제 서비스에 적용하기 전에, 요구하는 검색 품질과 응답 속도를 만족하려면 어느 정도의 물리 서버 자원이 필요한지 확인해야 했습니다. 서버가 부족하면 필요한 처리량과 응답 속도를 맞추기 어렵고, 과하게 준비하면 그만큼 비용이 늘어납니다. 토스증권은 온프레미스 중심으로 인프라를 운영하고 있어, 서비스를 올리기 전에 필요한 CPU와 메모리 규모를 가늠해야 했습니다. 그런데 같은 벡터 검색이라도 워크로드마다 조건이 달랐습니다. 사용하는 임베딩 모델에 따라 벡터 차원이 달랐고, 검색할 결과의 개수와 품질 목표, 데이터의 갱신 빈도도 달랐습니다. 공개 벤치마크의 QPS만으로는 이 조건들이 우리가 가지고 있는 장비에서 어떤 처리량과 지연시간을 보일지 알 수 없었어요. 서비스 요구사항과 모델의 사양, 인덱스 설정에 나뉘어 있는 정보를 모으고, 실제 자원 사용과 연결해 이해해야 했습니다. 저희는 인덱스와 검색 설정을 바꿔 가며 품질과 처리량을 비교했습니다. 검색 중 CPU와 메모리가 어떻게 쓰이는지도 들여다봤는데요. CPU와 메모리 배치를 조정하자 같은 서버에서 검색 품질을 유지하며 처리량을 41% 높일 수 있었습니다. 여기에 검색 설정과 벡터 차원, 서버 수를 바꿔 가며 측정한 결과를 더해 사이징 기준을 만들었습니다. 이번 글에서는 검색 조건을 정하는 것부터 CPU 내부를 살펴보고 워크로드에 필요한 서버 대수를 계산하기까지, 저희가 직접 확인한 내용을 공유하려고 합니다. 실험은 다음 순서로 진행했습니다. 그림 1. 검색 품질과 비교 조건을 정하고, CPU·메모리 배치를 개선한 뒤 서버 규모를 산정하는 과정 검색을 비교하기 전에 벡터 검색의 품질과 처리 성능 우리가 SQL에서 = 나 LIKE 로 검색할 때는 값이 일치하거나 문자열 패턴에 맞는 데이터를 찾습니다. 제품 설명에서 ‘배터리’라는 단어를 찾는다면, 그 단어가 없는 설명은 검색되지 않죠. 그런데 ‘배터리가 오래가는 휴대폰’을 찾는 사람에게는 ‘충전 없이 하루 종일 쓰는 스마트폰’이라는 설명도 유용한 결과일 수 있습니다. 그림 2. 텍스트·이미지·음성을 임베딩 모델로 변환한 벡터. 배열에 들어 있는 숫자의 개수가 차원입니다. 이렇게 표현이 달라도 의미가 비슷한 데이터를 찾는 데 벡터 검색을 활용할 수 있습니다. 임베딩 모델은 텍스트나 이미지, 음성을 숫자 배열인 벡터 로 변환하고, 비슷하다고 학습한 데이터를 벡터 공간에서 가까이 배치합니다. 이 배열에 들어 있는 숫자의 개수를 차원 이라고 부릅니다. 검색할 때는 검색어도 벡터로 변환합니다. 그리고 저장된 데이터의 벡터와 거리나 유사도를 비교해 가까운 결과부터 찾습니다. VectorDB는 이러한 검색을 위해 벡터를 식별자·메타데이터와 함께 저장하고 관리합니다. 그림 3. 검색어와 제품 설명을 벡터로 표현한 예시. 표현이 달라도 의미가 비슷한 데이터는 벡터 공간에서 가까이 놓일 수 있습니다. 실제 측정값이 아닌 개념도입니다. 저장된 모든 벡터와 거리를 비교하면 가장 가까운 결과를 정확히 구할 수 있습니다. 그런데 데이터가 수억 건이라면 검색할 때마다 전부 비교하기는 부담스럽겠죠. 그래서 모든 데이터를 확인하는 대신 탐색할 후보를 줄이는 ANN(Approximate Nearest Neighbor, 근사 최근접 이웃 검색) 을 사용합니다. 그만큼 계산은 줄어들지만, 전수 비교였다면 찾았을 결과를 일부 놓칠 수 있어요. 이번 실험에서 사용한 HNSW(Hierarchical Navigable Small World) 도 ANN 인덱스 중 하나입니다. 가까운 벡터를 여러 계층의 그래프로 연결하고, 성긴 상위 계층에서 검색 범위를 좁힌 뒤 모든 벡터가 있는 최하위 계층(Layer 0)에서 가까운 이웃을 탐색합니다. 그림 4. HNSW의 계층별 탐색 경로. 상위 계층에서 범위를 좁힌 뒤 Layer 0에서 이웃을 탐색합니다. 출처: Malkov & Yashunin, Figure 1. [1] ANN에서는 가까운 결과를 일부 놓칠 수 있기 때문에, 빨리 찾았다는 것만으로 검색을 평가하기는 어렵습니다. Milvus를 포함한 VectorDB의 ANN 검색에서 검색 품질과 처리 성능을 함께 보는 이유 입니다. 검색 품질(Quality) — 전수 비교로 구한 정답 집합을 ANN 검색이 얼마나 빠짐없이 찾았는지이며, recall 로 측정합니다. 정답 10개 중 9개를 찾으면 recall@10은 0.9입니다. 여기서 평가하는 것은 같은 벡터에서 가까운 이웃을 찾는 정확도이며, 임베딩 모델이 의미를 얼마나 잘 표현했는지는 별개입니다. 처리 성능(Performance) — 검색을 얼마나 많이, 얼마나 빠르게 처리하는지이며, QPS 와 지연시간(latency) 으로 측정합니다. 이 글에서 QPS는 초당 처리한 질의 벡터 수입니다. 한 요청에 여러 벡터를 담을 수 있으므로 초당 요청 수(RPS)와 구분합니다. 정답을 잘 찾더라도 응답이 느리거나 필요한 트래픽을 처리하지 못하면 서비스에서 쓰기 어렵습니다. 반대로 빠르게 처리하더라도 가까운 벡터를 많이 놓친다면 검색 결과를 쓰기 어렵고요. 저희에게는 둘 다 필요한 조건이었습니다. HNSW의 ef 설정에서 이 관계를 볼 수 있는데요. ef는 검색 후보의 범위를 조절하는 값입니다. 높이면 더 넓게 탐색하므로 대체로 recall이 좋아지지만, 시간과 연산도 더 필요해 처리량은 낮아질 수 있습니다. ef를 낮춰 얻은 높은 QPS라면, 그때 recall이 얼마나 떨어졌는지도 봐야 하는 거죠. 그래서 인덱스와 검색 설정을 비교할 때 사용할 최소 품질 기준을 정했습니다. 이번 실험에서는 recall@10 0.95 이상을 만족하는 설정에서 QPS와 지연시간을 비교 했습니다. 설정을 바꿔 QPS가 높아졌더라도 검색 품질이 함께 떨어졌다면 같은 조건의 개선으로 보지 않았습니다. 그림 5. recall@10 계산 예시. 정답 10개 중 9개를 찾았으므로 recall은 0.9입니다. Milvus를 선택한 이유 초기에는 Milvus와 Qdrant, Weaviate를 함께 검토했습니다. 그 과정에서 중요하게 본 것은 아키텍처였습니다. Milvus는 여러 노드가 검색을 나누어 처리하는 MPP(Massively Parallel Processing) 구조인데요. 검색과 데이터 적재, 인덱스 빌드를 담당하는 컴포넌트의 역할이 명확하게 나뉘어 있습니다. 요청은 Proxy가 받고, Coordinator가 작업을 조율하며, 워커가 실제 작업을 처리합니다. 워커도 맡는 일에 따라 나뉩니다. Milvus는 데이터를 세그먼트(segment) 라는 단위로 나누어 관리하는데요. 새 데이터가 추가되는 세그먼트를 growing , 더 이상 새 데이터를 추가하지 않도록 닫은 세그먼트를 sealed 라고 부릅니다. Milvus 2.6에서는 실시간 적재와 growing 세그먼트의 검색은 StreamingNode, sealed 세그먼트의 검색은 QueryNode, 인덱스 빌드와 compaction은 DataNode가 담당합니다. 클러스터 모드에서는 이 컴포넌트들을 독립적으로 배포하고 확장할 수 있어, 검색·적재·인덱스 빌드에 필요한 자원을 각각 조정할 수 있습니다. [2] 그림 6. Milvus 2.6 아키텍처. 실시간 적재·growing 데이터 검색은 StreamingNode, sealed 데이터 검색은 QueryNode, 인덱스 빌드·compaction은 DataNode가 담당합니다. [2] 검색 조건에 맞춰 인덱스와 하드웨어를 선택할 수 있는지도 중요하게 봤는데요. title: ARCS: Towards Precise Text-to-SQL via Structured Disambiguation
abstract: As text-to-SQL systems move beyond demonstrations toward real-world deployment, ambiguity in user questions becomes a primary source of errors. Such ambiguities are often subtle, domain- or data-specific, and can silently cause system outputs to deviate from the user's true intent. Ambiguity is traditionally addressed through conversational clarification, which is often inefficient, cognitively demanding, and poorly aligned with real-world user workflows. We propose structured disambiguation, a new paradigm in which ambiguity is resolved through explicit, constrained interactions rather than free-form dialogue. We construct ARCS (Ambiguity Resolution Corpus for SQL), the first text-to-SQL benchmark featuring naturally occurring, unconstrained ambiguities over real-world databases, with complete annotations of all valid ambiguity points, interpretations, and SQL queries. Experimental results show that text-to-SQL remains challenging in the presence of ambiguity: gpt-6-sol achieves only 51% end-to-end execution accuracy, and no open-source model exceeds 27%.

title: Relevance Does Not Imply Applicability: Experience Activation for Personal GUI Agents
abstract: Personal Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents rely on interaction history to infer what a user wants from ambiguous instructions and to anticipate recurring routines. Existing approaches retrieve task-relevant history and append it to the policy's context, implicitly assuming that experience relevant to a task remains useful for each decision within it. We find that this help is largely spent at the first decision: retrieved history strongly improves the opening step of an episode, yet provides little sustained benefit over the remaining 90\% of steps, and offers weak guidance on whether a proactive suggestion is warranted. A relevant record may tell the agent where to begin, but not which past action applies to the current screen or whether a routine is due now. The underlying issue is that relevance does not imply applicability}: relevance is determined at the task level, whereas applicability depends on the situation at decision time. We therefore recast personalization as experience activation and introduce ExpActivator, a training-free framework that activates only the experience applicable to the current situation. During execution, ExpActivator matches each new screen to historical states in the frozen GUI backbone's latent space and supplies the corresponding action as a reference. Before execution, it activates a recurring intent only when the current time and scenario provide sufficient support, and otherwise abstains. Across four GUI backbones, ExpActivator improves within-trajectory step success by 28\% on average, achieves the best personalized execution on every backbone while using about one-fifth as many history tokens, and reaches approximately 2.3times the Matthews correlation coefficient of the strongest proactive baseline. Experience pays where it is activated, not where it is appended.

title: Thinking Inertia: LLMs Keep Thinking When Told Not To
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly ship with explicit "thinking modes", yet their counterpart, "no-thinking", has received far less attention. We study LLMs' no-thinking behavior along two axes. a. How to measure no-thinking? Prior work typically defines no-thinking through proxies such as a disabled thinking mode or the absence of long traces. These proxies are unreliable: disabled thinking modes may still emit reasoning, while long traces may contain filler rather than genuine inference. We instead normalize each response into a pre-answer trace and final answer, and evaluate it at three levels: (i) Empty-Thinking Rate for strict answer-only compliance; (ii) instruction-aware Question-Pre-answer Relevance for similarity between the question and pre-answer trace; and (iii) LLM-as-judge Explicit Inference Rate for visible explicit inference. Together, these metrics distinguish answer-only output, relevant but non-inferential text, and explicit inference. b. How does no-thinking vary across tasks and models? We evaluate six prompting interventions on six LLMs across Boolean, multiple-choice, and open-ended questions. We find that explicit no-think controls cannot reliably eliminate visible inference. Models instead exhibit "Thinking Inertia": explicit inference persists even under strict controls and becomes more prevalent as the answer space opens. Accuracy remains stable on Boolean and multiple-choice tasks, whereas open-ended tasks reveal a trade-off between answer-only compliance and task accuracy. Rewriting the same questions across answer spaces shows that supplying candidate answers makes answer-only responses easier to produce. These findings establish no-thinking as a non-trivial capability: stopping explicit reasoning cannot be assumed from model settings or instructions alone and deserves systematic evaluation alongside reasoning ability.

title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? We term this ability Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM), an intrinsic component of visual intelligence that remains substantially underdeveloped in current LVLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SpatialASM, a scalable framework to internalize ASM into LVLMs through training-time spatial simulation. SpatialASM employs an allocentric novel-view generator to ground hypothetical viewpoints in visual evidence and produces two complementary forms of supervision: i) explicit ASM trajectories that teach LVLMs when and how to adaptively invoke view planning and imagination during spatial reasoning, and ii) automatically-constructed perspective-taking tasks that further strengthens viewpoint-conditioned scene imagination. On seven benchmarks spanning relatively perception-oriented spatial understanding to more challenging tasks requiring multi-image, cross-view and viewpoint-transformation reasoning, SpatialASM yields performance gain on LVLMs of four LVLM backbones in spatial reasoning while retaining their original general vision capabilities. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves average accuracy across the seven spatial benchmarks. And the synthesis of ASM trajectories provides a scalable pathway to alleviate the scarcity of spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision for eliciting active viewpoint exploration and mental scene simulation.

title: Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation: Formulation, Benchmark, and Method
abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) has largely focused on a single agent following a single instruction, yet many real-world applications require teams of robots to tackle tasks beyond the capabilities of any individual agent. We present Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation, providing, to our knowledge, the first systematic formalization of multi-agent VLN as a constrained coordination problem: each mission consists of subtasks carrying dependency and resource constraints (presence locks and holding chains). A verified four-stage crafting pipeline instantiates the task as MAVLN, comprising 11,724 episodes across 145 scenes with teams of up to four agents under three instruction regimes, accompanied by tailored constraint-aware metrics. We further present TRISS, a coordination-ready navigation system coupling an LLM-based subtask scheduler, a shared topological memory that turns each agent's exploration into team knowledge, and a conflict-aware execution mechanism that realizes simultaneous intentions as collision-free routes. Extensive experiments establish TRISS as a comprehensive baseline and reveal substantial room for improvement across scheduling, planning, and execution, highlighting the challenges of coordinating under MAVLN task constraints. Project page: https://xyz9911.github.io/mavln.

title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals
abstract: Attention Residuals (AttnRes) enables content-dependent retrieval over network depth, which can be viewed as single-stream softmax attention along the depth axis. Inspired by the success of multi-head attention along the sequence axis, we introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), an extension of AttnRes that generalizes this mechanism to multi-head depth attention, yielding substantial performance gains with minimal additional overhead. MSAR draws stream diversity from sequence context through multi-scale causal convolutions, allowing different heads to retrieve historical representations through distinct contextual views while preserving the integrity of the hidden representation. The retrieved streams are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to generate the single-stream layer input. By retaining single-stream sources and expanding them on demand, MSAR supports multi-stream computation without requiring persistent multi-stream storage or communication. Across all 12 downstream benchmarks at the 18B and 28B MoE scales, MSAR consistently outperforms prior residual variants, including standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes. Scaling-law experiments yield an iso-loss compute speedup of 1.58times over the standard residual baseline, compared with 1.35times for AttnRes and 1.30times for mHC. These results make MSAR a promising residual architecture for large-scale pre-training.

title: Humanity's Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models
abstract: Humans perceive far more in a scene than what is explicitly depicted: a single glance captures past causes and future trajectories; a quick peek determines if a vehicle can fit between two parked cars; a few seconds of video reveals who holds authority in a room; and a fleeting clip highlights subtle abstract patterns like unwritten rules or hidden labels. This capacity reflects a form of humanity's sixth sense: an intuitive reasoning mechanism that recovers implicit information beyond raw sensory perception. Crucially, this rapid, zero-shot visual intuition underpins everyday navigation and social interaction, making it a vital capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) deployed alongside people. Existing visual benchmarks, however, target either deliberate expert-level analysis in academic and mathematical domains or low-level perception, leaving the intuitive reasoning that people perform largely untested. To bridge this gap, we introduce Humanity's Sixth Sense (HSS), a benchmark for intuitive visual reasoning. HSS spans diverse image and video inputs, organizes items under a structured taxonomy, and pairs each with human-written prompts probing the implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract structure that people infer at a glance. Frontier MLLMs fall short of human performance: participants reach 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest model, GPT-6-astra, reaches only 53.6% even at maximum reasoning effort. Despite excelling in many complex tasks that require advanced perception and knowledge, current models still struggle significantly on these visual tasks that are intuitive for humans. We further explore agentic setup that apply dynamic visual manipulation to HSS, which narrows but does not close the gap. HSS establishes intuitive visual reasoning as a measurable axis and directs attention to a capability that scaling on current benchmarks has so far left behind.

title: Mental-Models for Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Large foundation models have accelerated progress toward general-purpose agents that interact with humans and other agents through language and multimodal signals. However, robust multi-agent decision-making requires reasoning about what other agents know, intend, and are likely to do under partial observability. Current agentic systems often operate through prompt design, memory, or end-to-end behavioral shaping, but typically do not learn an explicit partner-state representation that can be reused as a decision variable across tasks. We introduce mental-model-enabled agents, a framework that equips an agent with a latent mental model of its counterpart, allowing it to infer hidden beliefs, intentions, and likely reactions from the observed history and use these inferences to guide action selection. Our method learns an amortized recursive Theory-of-Mind representation, with first- and second-order mental-state structure, jointly with a belief-conditioned reward model that evaluates candidate actions relative to the inferred partner state. A policy is then learned under this belief-aware signal, yielding an agent that can act independently at inference time while retaining the benefits of explicit partner modeling. We evaluate the same framework on both language-only and multimodal benchmarks. Across these settings, explicit mental-state modeling consistently improves interaction quality and Theory-of-Mind performance over base agentic systems, showing that structured partner modeling is a useful inductive bias for general multi-agent systems. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/hananshafi/Mental-Models

title: BudgetPix: Compute-Adaptive Tokenization for Pixel-Space Image Diffusion
abstract: Most image generation models rely on uniform tokenization, allocating the exact same computational budget to equally-sized image patches. This static paradigm cannot adapt to different resource constraints at inference time, and yields suboptimal quality-cost tradeoff by devoting the same effort to both plain backgrounds and intricate details. We propose BudgetPix, an adaptive tokenization framework that dynamically allocates compute based on visual complexity and spatial layout, enabling flexible computational budgeting at inference time. BudgetPix comprises three key components: (1) an adaptive encoder that maps a fixed-size image to a variable-length token sequence using an entropy-guided quadtree alongside a multi-scale patch embedder; (2) a scale-aware decoder reconstructs fixed-resolution images from multi-scale token sets; and (3) a flexible training and sampling schedule that enables pixel-space denoisers to operate across variable token counts. BudgetPix seamlessly integrates with existing pixel-space diffusion architectures, enabling a single checkpoint to be operated at a wide range of compute budgets. Evaluated on text-to-image generation, BudgetPix matches the fidelity of MiniT2I-L at 512^2 and PixelDiT at 1024^2 using just 25% of the original compute budget. In class-conditional generation using a MeanFlow backbone, BudgetPix requires merely 60% of the full compute budget to produce images with near-zero quality degradation, observing a marginal 0.8-point increase in FID. Comprehensive assessments by human and VLM judges confirm that BudgetPix establishes a significantly improved quality-efficiency tradeoff over prior budget-adaptive baselines. More details are available at our project page: https://karaozgur.com/BudgetPix

title: Clinician use of language models diverges from how the models are evaluated
abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants are being deployed to clinicians across health systems, and judgments about their readiness rest largely on benchmark scores, most of them derived from examination questions or curated cases. A benchmark predicts performance in deployment only to the extent that its items resemble real use, yet whether benchmarks reflect the work these systems receive has rarely been measured. Here we analyze 127,833 queries sent by 6,342 physicians, advanced practice providers and nurses in 35 specialties to an institutional assistant during an eight-month roll-out. We characterize each query with RCQ-Map, a clinician-validated framework grounded in taxonomies of clinical questions and of LLM evaluation, which records its task, intent, answerability, missing information and potential harm. Documentation and administration (36.2%) and knowledge retrieval (28.9%) made up nearly two-thirds of use, and diagnosis 3.7%; more than a third of queries could not be answered well as posed. Applying RCQ-Map to 58 public benchmarks drawn from major evaluation suites and frontier model reports, which we assemble into the Clinical AI Benchmark Atlas, showed that the median benchmark contained no documentation requests and shared 31% of the task mix of real use, less than an even spread across task categories would. Benchmarks in suites designed to resemble clinical practice were individually no closer to real use than those used in frontier model reports. Benchmark scores therefore say little about how clinical AI performs on most of the work it is actually given, and evaluation should be matched to real clinical use.

title: Video-Conditioned Generative Joint 2D-3D Hand Motion Recovery
abstract: Recovering faithful 3D hand motion from video remains challenging due to frequent occlusions and incomplete visual observations, which make frame-wise pose estimates unreliable and temporally inconsistent. To address this problem, we propose JoHan, a unified generative framework that recovers hand motion directly from video sequences without relying on intermediate per-frame pose predictions. Trained from scratch, our model jointly generates aligned 2D and 3D local hand pose sequences by learning their temporal dynamics and cross-representation correspondence. The generated 2D trajectories exploit direct spatial and temporal cues from the 2D images to guide the following generative 3D motion reconstruction, while the learned motion prior promotes temporal consistency. Their learned 2D-3D correspondence further enables recovery of the hand's global position and orientation relative to the camera. Extensive experiments on challenging benchmarks demonstrate significantly improved accuracy and speed in local hand-pose and camera-space reconstruction. Notably, our method captures much better hand-motion dynamics, producing significantly smoother motion than previous methods while maintaining high per-frame pose accuracy.

title: Few-Step Generation via Data-Space Iteration
abstract: Flow matching has emerged as a scalable paradigm for training high-quality generative models, but sampling from the learned probability flow requires many network evaluations.
